title: Structuring API Requests
summary: Covers the three parts of an API request URL: the endpoint, query parameters and path parameters, and distinguishes private from public APIs. Three Postman exercises against the course's Bored API practise each: GET /random, filter by type and participants, and fetch one activity by key.

concepts.heading: Private vs public APIs
points: Your own front end calling your own server is effectively a private API: undocumented and meant only for your client.
A public API is one a provider deliberately exposes and documents so other developers' servers can request data or actions.
This module is about consuming public APIs from your own server code.
The practice API is the course's Bored API (bored-api.appbrewery.com), holding activities with fields such as type, participants, price and a unique key.

concepts.heading: Endpoints
points: URL structure: base URL, then a forward slash, then an endpoint. Each endpoint is a fixed route for a purpose, for example /random for a random activity and /filter for filtered lists.
Docs normally give an example request and sample response for each endpoint. Always read them first.
Public APIs often rate-limit to prevent abuse; this one allows about 100 requests per 15 minutes. If you get a too-many-requests response, wait.
Exercise 1: send GET base-URL/random in Postman; each send returns a different activity.

concepts.heading: Query parameters
points: Appended after the endpoint to add optional key/value information, mostly for filtering, sorting and searching.
Syntax: start with ?, write key=value, and join further pairs with &, for example ?a=1&b=2&c=3.
Parameter names are exact and come from the docs (the filter endpoint takes participants in the plural).
Postman's Params table builds the URL from key/value rows. In server code you must build the query string yourself, so practise typing it.
Exercise 2: GET /filter?type=social&participants=2 returns social activities for two people. The docs list the seven allowed type values.

concepts.heading: Path parameters
points: A variable segment placed after a slash in the path, used to identify one specific resource such as an ID or username.
Contrast: query parameters filter or search across many results; path parameters pinpoint a single item.
Every activity has a unique key. Request GET /activity/<key> to fetch that one, e.g. the movie marathon activity with key 5914292.
Handy when your site must always show a specific item.

concepts.heading: Next up
points: The following lesson covers JSON, the usual format of API responses.

task.name: Three Bored API requests in Postman
task.starting_point: Postman open and the Bored API documentation page.
task.goal: Practise endpoint, query parameter and path parameter requests.
steps: Create a GET request to the base URL plus /random and send it repeatedly to see different activities.
Create a GET to /filter, add type=social and participants=2 (first with the Params table, then by typing ?type=social&participants=2 yourself).
Copy an activity's key from a response and GET /activity/<key> to retrieve exactly that activity.
task.expected_result: A random activity per request; a filtered list of social two-person activities; and one specific activity matching the key.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 28 - Aplication Programming Interfaces (APIs)/28.02 - Structuring API Requests/API Endpoints.png, Multiple Query Parameters.png, Path Parameters.png

pitfalls: Using a second ? instead of & for later query parameters.
Misspelling parameter names such as participant vs participants.
Exceeding the rate limit while testing.
Confusing path and query parameters: use query for filtering, path for identifying one resource.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Structuring API requests': blurb on endpoint, query and path parameters.
Tasks: (1) label parts of a URL, (2) build a filter URL with two query params, (3) fetch /random and render the activity, (4) fetch by key via a path parameter.
Starter idea: a fetch against the Bored API with a result div.
Interactive demo: a URL builder where editing fields updates a coloured URL and fires the request.
